name: Data Obfuscation
summary: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.

name: Junk Data
summary: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.

name: Steganography
summary: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult.

name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
summary: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts.

name: Data Compressed
summary: An adversary may compress data (e.g., sensitive documents) that is collected prior to exfiltration in order to make it portable and minimize the amount of data sent over the network.

name: OS Credential Dumping
summary: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password.

name: LSASS Memory
summary: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS).

name: Security Account Manager
summary: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored.

name: NTDS
summary: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and access rights.

name: LSA Secrets
summary: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts.

name: Cached Domain Credentials
summary: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.

name: DCSync
summary: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain controller using a technique called DCSync.

name: Proc Filesystem
summary: Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or /proc.

name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
summary: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking.

name: Winlogon Helper DLL
summary: Winlogon.exe is a Windows component responsible for actions at logon/logoff as well as the secure attention sequence (SAS) triggered by Ctrl-Alt-Delete.

name: Data from Local System
summary: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

name: Direct Volume Access
summary: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring.

name: System Service Discovery
summary: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services.

name: Fallback Channels
summary: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

name: Binary Padding
summary: Adversaries can use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware without affecting the functionality or behavior of the binary.

name: Application Window Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows.

name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel.

name: Query Registry
summary: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

name: Port Monitors
summary: A port monitor can be set through the API call to set a DLL to be loaded at startup.

name: Rootkit
summary: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components.

name: Accessibility Features
summary: Windows contains accessibility features that may be launched with a key combination before a user has logged in (for example, when the user is on the Windows logon screen).

name: System Network Configuration Discovery
summary: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems.

name: Internet Connection Discovery
summary: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems.

name: Wi-Fi Discovery
summary: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems.

name: Application Deployment Software
summary: Adversaries may deploy malicious software to systems within a network using application deployment systems employed by enterprise administrators.

name: Remote System Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system.

name: System Firmware
summary: The BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) and The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) or Extensible Firmware Interface (EFI) are examples of system firmware that operate as the software interface between the operating system and hardware of a computer.

name: Automated Exfiltration
summary: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.

name: Traffic Duplication
summary: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure.

name: Remote Services
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC.

name: Remote Desktop Protocol
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).

name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB).

name: Distributed Component Object Model
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM).

name: SSH
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH).

name: VNC
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).

name: Windows Remote Management
summary: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM).

name: Cloud Services
summary: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities.

name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
summary: Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods.

name: Data Encrypted
summary: Data is encrypted before being exfiltrated in order to hide the information that is being exfiltrated from detection or to make the exfiltration less conspicuous upon inspection by a defender.

name: Shortcut Modification
summary: Shortcuts or symbolic links are ways of referencing other files or programs that will be opened or executed when the shortcut is clicked or executed by a system startup process.

name: Custom Cryptographic Protocol
summary: Adversaries may use a custom cryptographic protocol or algorithm to hide command and control traffic.

name: Data from Removable Media
summary: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

name: Multiband Communication
summary: **This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.** Some adversaries may split communications between different protocols.

name: Obfuscated Files or Information
summary: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit.

name: Binary Padding
summary: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware.

name: Software Packing
summary: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code.

name: Steganography
summary: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information.

name: Compile After Delivery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code.

name: Indicator Removal from Tools
summary: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed.

name: HTML Smuggling
summary: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files.

name: Dynamic API Resolution
summary: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis.

name: Stripped Payloads
summary: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information.

name: Embedded Payloads
summary: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses.

name: Command Obfuscation
summary: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection.

name: Fileless Storage
summary: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses.

name: LNK Icon Smuggling
summary: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files.

name: Encrypted/Encoded File
summary: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection.

name: Polymorphic Code
summary: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection.

name: Compression
summary: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files.

name: Junk Code Insertion
summary: Adversaries may use junk code / dead code to obfuscate a malware's functionality.

name: SVG Smuggling
summary: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign SVG files.

name: Invisible Unicode
summary: Adversaries may abuse invisible or non-printing Unicode characters to conceal malicious content within files, scripts, or text.

name: Windows Remote Management
summary: Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).

name: Scheduled Transfer
summary: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals.

name: Data Transfer Size Limits
summary: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds.

name: Modify Existing Service
summary: Windows service configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable or recovery programs/commands, is stored in the Registry.

name: Standard Cryptographic Protocol
summary: Adversaries may explicitly employ a known encryption algorithm to conceal command and control traffic rather than relying on any inherent protections provided by a communication protocol.

name: System Owner/User Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to identify the primary user, currently logged in user, set of users that commonly uses a system, or whether a user is actively using the system.

name: Path Interception
summary: **This technique has been deprecated.

name: Service Execution
summary: Adversaries may execute a binary, command, or script via a method that interacts with Windows services, such as the Service Control Manager.

name: Masquerading
summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

name: Invalid Code Signature
summary: Adversaries may attempt to mimic features of valid code signatures to increase the chance of deceiving a user, analyst, or tool.

name: Right-to-Left Override
summary: Adversaries may abuse the right-to-left override (RTLO or RLO) character (U+202E) to disguise a string and/or file name to make it appear benign.

name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
summary: Adversaries may rename legitimate / system utilities to try to evade security mechanisms concerning the usage of those utilities.

name: Masquerade Task or Service
summary: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate the name of a task or service to make it appear legitimate or benign.

name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
summary: Adversaries may match or approximate the name or location of legitimate files, Registry keys, or other resources when naming/placing them.

name: Space after Filename
summary: Adversaries can hide a program's true filetype by changing the extension of a file.

name: Double File Extension
summary: Adversaries may abuse a double extension in the filename as a means of masquerading the true file type.

name: Masquerade File Type
summary: Adversaries may masquerade malicious payloads as legitimate files through changes to the payload's formatting, including the file's signature, extension, icon, and contents.

name: Break Process Trees
summary: An adversary may attempt to evade process tree-based analysis by modifying executed malware's parent process ID (PPID).

name: Masquerade Account Name
summary: Adversaries may match or approximate the names of legitimate accounts to make newly created ones appear benign.

name: Overwrite Process Arguments
summary: Adversaries may modify a process's in-memory arguments to change its name in order to appear as a legitimate or benign process.

name: Browser Fingerprint
summary: Adversaries may attempt to blend in with legitimate traffic by spoofing browser and system attributes like operating system, system language, platform, user-agent string, resolution, time zone, etc.

name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
summary: Adversaries may use scripts automatically executed at boot or logon initialization to establish persistence.

name: Logon Script (Windows)
summary: Adversaries may use Windows logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

name: Login Hook
summary: Adversaries may use a Login Hook to establish persistence executed upon user logon.

name: Network Logon Script
summary: Adversaries may use network logon scripts automatically executed at logon initialization to establish persistence.

name: RC Scripts
summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by modifying RC scripts, which are executed during a Unix-like system's startup.

name: Startup Items
summary: Adversaries may use startup items automatically executed at boot initialization to establish persistence.

name: DLL Search Order Hijacking
summary: Windows systems use a common method to look for required DLLs to load into a program.

name: Data from Network Shared Drive
summary: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

name: Network Sniffing
summary: Adversaries may passively sniff network traffic to capture information about an environment, including authentication material passed over the network.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel.

name: Change Default File Association
summary: When a file is opened, the default program used to open the file (also called the file association or handler) is checked.

name: Commonly Used Port
summary: **This technique has been deprecated.

name: File System Permissions Weakness
summary: Processes may automatically execute specific binaries as part of their functionality or to perform other actions.

name: Software Packing
summary: Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable.

name: Network Service Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of services running on remote hosts and local network infrastructure devices, including those that may be vulnerable to remote software exploitation.

name: Windows Management Instrumentation
summary: Adversaries may abuse Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute malicious commands and payloads.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
summary: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel.

name: System Network Connections Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of network connections to or from the compromised system they are currently accessing or from remote systems by querying for information over the network.

name: New Service
summary: When operating systems boot up, they can start programs or applications called services that perform background system functions.

name: Shared Webroot

name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive.

name: Exfiltration over USB
summary: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device.

name: Scheduled Task/Job
summary: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

name: At (Linux)
summary: Adversaries may abuse the at utility to perform task scheduling for initial, recurring, or future execution of malicious code.

name: At
summary: Adversaries may abuse the at utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

name: Cron
summary: Adversaries may abuse the cron utility to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

name: Launchd
summary: This technique is deprecated due to the inaccurate usage.

name: Scheduled Task
summary: Adversaries may abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

name: Systemd Timers
summary: Adversaries may abuse systemd timers to perform task scheduling for initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

name: Container Orchestration Job
summary: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality provided by container orchestration tools such as Kubernetes to schedule deployment of containers configured to execute malicious code.

name: Indicator Blocking
summary: An adversary may attempt to block indicators or events typically captured by sensors from being gathered and analyzed.

name: Process Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject code into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Dynamic-link Library Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Portable Executable Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject portable executables (PE) into processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Thread Execution Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Asynchronous Procedure Call
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Thread Local Storage
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via thread local storage (TLS) callbacks in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Ptrace System Calls
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via ptrace (process trace) system calls in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Proc Memory
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via the /proc filesystem in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Extra Window Memory Injection
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via Extra Window Memory (EWM) in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Process Hollowing
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into suspended and hollowed processes in order to evade process-based defenses.

name: Process Doppelgänging
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into process via process doppelgänging in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: VDSO Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may inject malicious code into processes via VDSO hijacking in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: ListPlanting
summary: Adversaries may abuse list-view controls to inject malicious code into hijacked processes in order to evade process-based defenses as well as possibly elevate privileges.

name: Input Capture

name: Keylogging

name: GUI Input Capture
summary: Adversaries may mimic common operating system GUI components to prompt users for credentials with a seemingly legitimate prompt.

name: Web Portal Capture
summary: Adversaries may install code on externally facing portals, such as a VPN login page, to capture and transmit credentials of users who attempt to log into the service.

name: Credential API Hooking
summary: Adversaries may hook into Windows application programming interface (API) functions and Linux system functions to collect user credentials.

name: Process Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get information about running processes on a system.

name: Service Registry Permissions Weakness
summary: Windows stores local service configuration information in the Registry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services.

name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
summary: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries.

name: PowerShell

name: AppleScript
summary: Adversaries may abuse AppleScript for execution.

name: Windows Command Shell

name: Unix Shell
summary: Adversaries may abuse Unix shell commands and scripts for execution.

name: Visual Basic

name: Python
summary: Adversaries may abuse Python commands and scripts for execution.

name: JavaScript
summary: Adversaries may abuse various implementations of JavaScript for execution.

name: Network Device CLI
summary: Adversaries may abuse scripting or built-in command line interpreters (CLI) on network devices to execute malicious command and payloads.

name: Cloud API
summary: Adversaries may abuse cloud APIs to execute malicious commands.

name: AutoHotKey & AutoIT
summary: Adversaries may execute commands and perform malicious tasks using AutoIT and AutoHotKey automation scripts.

name: Lua
summary: Adversaries may abuse Lua commands and scripts for execution.

name: Hypervisor CLI

name: Container CLI/API

name: Scripting

summary: A bootkit is a malware variant that modifies the boot sectors of a hard drive, including the Master Boot Record (MBR) and Volume Boot Record (VBR).

name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
summary: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in an attempt to elevate privileges.

name: Permission Groups Discovery
summary: Adversaries may attempt to discover group and permission settings.

name: Local Groups
summary: Adversaries may attempt to find local system groups and permission settings.

name: Domain Groups
summary: Adversaries may attempt to find domain-level groups and permission settings.

name: Cloud Groups
summary: Adversaries may attempt to find cloud groups and permission settings.

name: Indicator Removal
summary: Adversaries may selectively delete or modify artifacts generated to reduce indications of their presence and blend in with legitimate activity.

name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
summary: Adversaries may clear system logs to hide evidence of an intrusion.

name: Clear Command History
summary: In addition to clearing system logs, an adversary may clear the command history of a compromised account to conceal the actions undertaken during an intrusion.

name: File Deletion
summary: Adversaries may delete files left behind by the actions of their intrusion activity.

name: Network Share Connection Removal
summary: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation.

name: Timestomp

name: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
summary: Adversaries may clear or remove evidence of malicious network connections in order to clean up traces of their operations.

name: Clear Mailbox Data

name: Clear Persistence
summary: Adversaries may clear artifacts associated with previously established persistence on a host system to remove evidence of their activity.

name: Relocate Malware

name: Remote Desktop Protocol
summary: Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems.

name: Default Accounts
summary: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of a default account as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

name: Domain Accounts

summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of domain accounts.

name: Email Account
summary: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of email addresses and accounts.

name: Cloud Account

name: Reflection Amplification

name: Endpoint Denial of Service

name: OS Exhaustion Flood

name: Service Exhaustion Flood

name: Application Exhaustion Flood

name: Application or System Exploitation

name: Compile After Delivery

name: Systemd Service

name: Parent PID Spoofing

name: PowerShell Profile

name: Web Shell

name: Backup Software Discovery

name: Cloud Instance Metadata API

name: Cloud Service Discovery

name: Steal Application Access Token

name: Unused/Unsupported Cloud Regions

name: Cloud Service Dashboard

name: Steal Web Session Cookie
summary: An adversary may steal web application or service session cookies and use them to gain access to web applications or Internet services as an authenticated user without needing credentials.

name: Bootkit

name: Launch Agent

name: Emond
summary: Adversaries may gain persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by the Event Monitor Daemon (emond).

name: Component Object Model Hijacking
summary: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by hijacked references to Component Object Model (COM) objects.

name: Installer Packages
summary: Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by using an installer to trigger the execution of malicious content.

name: Udev Rules
summary: Adversaries may maintain persistence through executing malicious content triggered using udev rules.

name: Python Startup Hooks
summary: Adversaries may achieve persistence by leveraging Python's startup mechanisms, including path configuration (.pth) files and the sitecustomize.py or usercustomize.py modules.

summary: Adversaries may configure system settings to automatically execute a program during system boot or logon to maintain persistence or gain higher-level privileges on compromised systems.

name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder

name: Authentication Package
summary: Adversaries may abuse authentication packages to execute DLLs when the system boots.

name: Time Providers
summary: Adversaries may abuse time providers to execute DLLs when the system boots.

name: Winlogon Helper DLL
summary: Adversaries may abuse features of Winlogon to execute DLLs and/or executables when a user logs in.

name: Security Support Provider

name: Kernel Modules and Extensions
summary: Adversaries may modify the kernel to automatically execute programs on system boot.

name: Re-opened Applications

name: LSASS Driver

name: Shortcut Modification

name: Port Monitors

name: Plist Modification

name: Bypass User Account Control

name: Sudo and Sudo Caching

name: Elevated Execution with Prompt
summary: Adversaries may leverage the AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API to escalate privileges by prompting the user for credentials.

name: Temporary Elevated Cloud Access

name: TCC Manipulation

name: Pass the Hash

name: Pass the Ticket

name: Web Session Cookie
summary: Adversaries can use stolen session cookies to authenticate to web applications and services.

name: Credentials In Files

name: Credentials in Registry
summary: Adversaries may search the Registry on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

name: Shell History
summary: Adversaries may search the command history on compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials.

name: Private Keys

name: Cloud Instance Metadata API
summary: Adversaries may attempt to access the Cloud Instance Metadata API to collect credentials and other sensitive data.

name: Group Policy Preferences
summary: Adversaries may attempt to find unsecured credentials in Group Policy Preferences (GPP).

name: Container API

name: Chat Messages

name: Subvert Trust Controls
summary: Adversaries may undermine security controls that will either warn users of untrusted activity or prevent execution of untrusted programs.

name: Code Signing
summary: Adversaries may create, acquire, or steal code signing materials to sign their malware or tools.

summary: Adversaries may tamper with SIP and trust provider components to mislead the operating system and application control tools when conducting signature validation checks.

name: Install Root Certificate
summary: Adversaries may install a root certificate on a compromised system to avoid warnings when connecting to adversary controlled web servers.

name: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
summary: Adversaries may abuse specific file formats to subvert Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) controls.

name: Network Provider DLL

name: Conditional Access Policies

name: Safe Mode Boot
